title: About This Graphic
text:
This project compares observation timelines and tracking patterns between two marine species in very different ocean environments:

Whale Sharks (Rhincodon typus) in the Coral Sea (Australia): 2,391 observations collected by the Biopixel Oceans Foundation and James Cook University, combining satellite tag transmissions from 18 named whale sharks (such as Megashark, Alexios, Ali, and Sharpie) with 136 opportunistic Coral Sea sightings.
Beluga Whales (Delphinapterus leucas) in the Western Beaufort Sea (Arctic): 1,244 acoustic detections recorded by a moored underwater hydrophone (Aural_M2) from the University of Washington between September 2010 and August 2011.

title: About This Graphic
text:
How to Read the Graphic

Horizontal Axis (X-Axis) — Observation Date Span Elapsed (Days Since First Sighting):
Measures how many days have passed since that specific individual shark (or the Beaufort Sea mooring) was first recorded. Placing every track on a “Days Since First Sighting” scale lets us directly compare observation durations even when the recordings occurred in different calendar years.
Vertical Axis (Y-Axis) — Cumulative Spotting / Tracking Count:
Counts each new detection in chronological order (\(1, 2, 3, \dots, N\)). A steep upward curve means frequent detections over a short period, while a flatter curve means detections were spread out over a longer time span.
Color Grouping:
Dark teal points represent Whale Shark Trackings (Coral Sea) and light blue points represent Beluga Whale Detections (Beaufort Sea).

title: About This Graphic
text:
What Happens in the Plot

Seasonal Bursts in Beluga Detections (Light Blue Curve):
The Beluga Whale acoustic curve climbs to 1,244 detections over roughly 331 days. Rather than rising at a constant rate, it shows steep steps during autumn and summer migration windows through the Beaufort Sea, separated by a flat horizontal gap during the mid-winter months when Belugas move away from heavy pack ice.
Individual Whale Shark Trajectories (Dark Teal Curves):
Each tagged whale shark forms its own distinct trajectory starting at Day 0:

High-frequency satellite tracks like Megashark (423 transmissions over ~397 days) and Alexios (357 transmissions over ~158 days) climb rapidly as their satellite tags report locations regularly.
Multi-year tracks like Ali (273 transmissions across 770 days) and Blancpain (73 transmissions across 526 days) show intermittent bursts when the sharks surface long enough to transmit to satellites.
Opportunistic Coral Sea Sightings extend across more than 10 years (4,006 days), forming a long, gradual line across the bottom of the chart.

title: About This Graphic
text:
Using the Interactive Controls

Top Filter Sliders & Dropdown: Filter the points in real time by elapsed days, cumulative spotting count, or select a single named Whale Shark or the Beluga Whale dataset.
Timeframe View Menu (Top-Left of Plot): Switch between the full 4,006-day span, a log-scale X-axis that spreads short and long tracks evenly, or zoomed-in views of the 0–400 day overlap window.
Bottom Range Slider: Drag the handles at the bottom of the plot to zoom dynamically into any window of elapsed days.
